tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.name: ScheduleWakeup
tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

delaySeconds.description: Seconds from now to wake up. Clamped to [60, 3600] by the runtime. Required unless `stop` is true.

reason.description: One short sentence explaining the chosen delay. Goes to telemetry and is shown to the user. Be specific. Required unless `stop` is true.

prompt.description: The /loop input to fire on wake-up. Pass the same /loop input verbatim each turn so the next firing re-enters the skill and continues the loop. For autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` instead (the dynamic-pacing variant, not the CronCreate-mode `<<autonomous-loop>>`). Required unless `stop` is true.

stop.description: Set to true to end the dynamic loop immediately instead of scheduling another wakeup. When true, all other fields are ignored and no further wakeups fire.

noop.description: true = nothing changed (you checked and there is nothing to report). false = something happened worth keeping (edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, surfaced a finding). Consecutive noop:true ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak. Required unless `stop` is true.

tools.name: SendUserFile
tools.description:
Send files to the user. Use this for any file the user would want to see — a generated diagram, a report, a screenshot, a built artifact — and you want it surfaced, not just mentioned. Send deliverables as they are produced, not batched at the end of the task: a complete draft or a meaningfully updated version of the thing the user asked for is worth sending mid-task, so they can follow progress and redirect early. Do NOT send routine working files — scratch files, debug output, partial fragments, or every incremental save of something you're still actively editing; each call renders a file card in the conversation, and a stream of cards for one file is noise. Re-send a file only when it has meaningfully changed since the last send. Paths can be absolute or relative to the current working directory.

Add a `caption` when a one-liner of context helps ("the failing case is row 42", "before vs after"). Skip it if the file speaks for itself.

Set `status` on every call. Use `proactive` when you're initiating — the user is away and you want this to reach their phone (build artifact ready, report generated). Use `normal` when replying to something the user just said.

Set `display` to choose how the file is presented. Use `'render'` when the user should see the content inline in the side panel right now — a chart, a rendered HTML page, a diagram, an image. Use `'attach'` when the file is something they'll save and open elsewhere — source code, a spreadsheet, a document for another app — and an inline preview would just be noise. Leave it unset to let the client decide by file type.

Files must already exist on the local filesystem — the tool sends files, it doesn't fetch URLs or render content. When unsure of a path, verify with ls first; absolute paths avoid ambiguity about the working directory.

Example: SendUserFile({ files: ["report.md"], caption: "Here's the report.", status: "normal" })

tools.name: Skill
tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

tools.name: SuggestSkills
tools.description:
Render a card of standalone skills the user can add — org, shared, or Anthropic skills not yet enabled.

Call this when the task is one a skill could make repeatable — drafting in a house style, reviews against a playbook, a recurring workflow — and nothing enabled covers it; the user does not need to ask about skills. Also when they ask for recommendations, or when ListSkills returned zero matches. Use ListSkills for skills they already have.

Do NOT call this for one-off questions you can answer directly, when you are unsure a skill would help, or if you already rendered a suggestion this conversation and the user didn't engage.

Pass keywords drawn from the task itself, and set trigger ('proactive' when you initiated this from task context, 'user_asked' when they asked). If the result is empty and the trigger was proactive, continue the task without mentioning that you searched; if the user asked, tell them you found nothing new to add.

tools.name: ToolSearch
tools.description:
Fetches full schema definitions for deferred tools so they can be called.

Deferred tools appear by name in <system-reminder> messages. Until fetched, only the name is known — there is no parameter schema, so the tool cannot be invoked. This tool takes a query, matches it against the deferred tool list, and returns the matched tools' complete JSONSchema definitions inside a <functions> block. Once a tool's schema appears in that result, it is callable exactly like any tool defined at the top of the prompt.

Result format: each matched tool appears as one <function>{"description": "...", "name": "...", "parameters": {...}}</function> line inside the <functions> block — the same encoding as the tool list at the top of this prompt.

Query forms:
- "select:Read,Edit,Grep" — fetch these exact tools by name
- "notebook jupyter" — keyword search, up to max_results best matches
- "+slack send" — require "slack" in the name, rank by remaining terms

tools.name: Workflow
tools.description:
Execute a workflow script that orchestrates multiple subagents deterministically. Workflows run in the background — this tool returns immediately with a task ID, and a <task-notification> arrives when the workflow completes. Use /workflows to watch live progress.

ONLY call this tool when the user has explicitly opted into multi-agent orchestration. Workflows can spawn dozens of agents and consume a large amount of tokens; the user must request that scale, not have it inferred. Explicit opt-in means one of:
- The user included the keyword "ultracode" in their prompt (you'll see a system-reminder confirming it).
- Ultracode is on for the session (a system-reminder confirms it) — see **Ultracode** in the workflow authoring reference.
- The user directly asked you to run a workflow or use multi-agent orchestration in their own words ("use a workflow", "run a workflow", "fan out agents", "orchestrate this with subagents"). The ask must be in the user's words — a task that would merely benefit from a workflow does not count.
- The user invoked a skill or slash command whose instructions tell you to call Workflow.
- The user asked you to run a specific named or saved workflow.

For any other task — even one that would clearly benefit from parallelism — do NOT call this tool. Use the Agent tool (if available) for individual subagents, or briefly describe what a multi-agent workflow could do and how much it would roughly cost, and ask the user whether to run it. Mention they can ask for one with "use a workflow" in a future message to skip the ask.

Every script must begin with `export const meta = {...}`: a PURE LITERAL (no variables, calls or interpolation) giving the workflow's `name`, a one-line `description` (shown in the permission dialog) and optionally `phases` — one `{ title, detail? }` per phase() call, titles matched exactly. Pass the script inline via `script` — do not Write it to a file first, and do not also set the tool's `name` input (that selects a saved workflow); it is plain JavaScript, not TypeScript.

The canonical multi-stage pattern — pipeline by default, each dimension verifies as soon as its review completes:
  export const meta = {
    name: 'review-changes',
    description: 'Review changed files across dimensions, verify each finding',
    phases: [{ title: 'Review' }, { title: 'Verify' }],
  }
  const DIMENSIONS = [{key: 'bugs', prompt: '...'}, {key: 'perf', prompt: '...'}]
  const results = await pipeline(
    DIMENSIONS,
    d => agent(d.prompt, {label: `review:${d.key}`, phase: 'Review', schema: FINDINGS_SCHEMA}),
    review => parallel(review.findings.map(f => () =>
      agent(`Adversarially verify: ${f.title}`, {label: `verify:${f.file}`, phase: 'Verify', schema: VERDICT_SCHEMA})
        .then(v => ({...f, verdict: v}))
    ))
  )
  const confirmed = results.flat().filter(Boolean).filter(f => f.verdict?.isReal)
  return { confirmed }
  // Dimension 'bugs' findings verify while dimension 'perf' is still reviewing. No wasted wall-clock.

Before writing a script, load the `workflow-authoring` skill — the workflow authoring reference: script API and gotchas, resume, the **Ultracode** section, quality patterns, worked examples.

This session has the default workflow size guideline: medium — keep workflows under 15 agents. This is a guideline, not a hard limit — follow it unless the user's prompt calls for a different scale. The user can raise or remove it with "Dynamic workflow size" in /config.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__dismiss_task
tools.description:
Withdraw a background-task chip you previously created with spawn_task.

Call this when a suggestion you flagged is now stale, superseded, or irrelevant — e.g. you (or the user) already fixed it in this session, or you spawned a better-scoped replacement. To replace a chip: call spawn_task with the new suggestion first, then dismiss the old task_id.

Only chips the user hasn't acted on can be withdrawn from the queue. If the user already started or dismissed the task, the result says so (a dismissed task's copy kept for later is withdrawn too) — do not retry.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__mark_chapter
tools.description:
Mark the start of a new chapter in this session.

Call this when the work shifts to a meaningfully different phase — e.g. after finishing exploration and starting implementation, after a fix lands and you move to verification, or when the user pivots to an unrelated request. The user sees a divider in the transcript and a floating table of contents for jumping between chapters.

Use sparingly: a chapter should cover a coherent stretch of work, not every tool call. A typical session has 3–8 chapters. Do not mark a chapter for the very first message — the session start is implicit.

The title is a short noun phrase ("Codebase exploration", "Auth bug fix", "Test verification"), not a sentence.

tools.name: mcp__ccd_session__spawn_task
tools.description:
Flag an out-of-scope issue for a separate background task.

Call this when you notice something worth fixing that would bloat the current change — dead code, stale docs, missing coverage, a confirmed TODO, or a security issue spotted in passing. Don't flag vague code-smell observations, trivial fixes you can do inline, or low-confidence hunches. A chip appears for the user; one click spins it off into its own session. Your current turn continues uninterrupted.

The prompt must stand alone — include file paths and enough context to act without this conversation.

The result includes a task_id; call dismiss_task with it if the suggestion later becomes stale.

tools.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__browser_batch
tools.description: Execute a sequence of Browser pane tool calls in ONE round trip. Each item is {name, input} where input is exactly what you'd pass to that tool standalone. Actions execute SEQUENTIALLY (not in parallel) and stop on the first error. Use this tool extensively to quickly execute work whenever you can predict two or more steps ahead — e.g. navigate, click a field, type, press Return, screenshot. Each tool's own permission check runs per item — a step on a site the user hasn't allowed either asks the user inline (and continues if they allow) or is refused, which stops the batch; if a step is refused for a missing permission, call that tool on its own (that call can ask the user), then batch the rest. Screenshots and other images are returned interleaved with outputs; coordinates you write in THIS batch refer to the screenshot taken BEFORE this call. browser_batch cannot be nested, and preview_start is not batchable — but if the Browser pane isn't open yet, a batch whose FIRST action is navigate with a url opens it (other actions still need an open page).

schema.name: mcp__Claude_Browser__computer
schema.description: Mouse/keyboard automation in the Browser pane. Clicks accept either `coordinate` (pixels in the coordinate frame of the most recent `computer{action:"screenshot"}` — reported with every scaled screenshot; equal to the image's pixels for unscaled ones) or `ref` (a `ref_N` from read_page/find). Whenever you intend to click on an element like an icon, you should consult a screenshot to determine the coordinates of the element first; after the tab loads a different site, take a new screenshot before clicking by `coordinate`.

tabId.description: Tab to act on within the preview context. Omit for the fronted tab; get ids from tabs_context.

action.description:
The action to perform:
* `left_click`: Click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `right_click`: Click the right mouse button at the specified coordinates to open context menus.
* `double_click`: Double-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `triple_click`: Triple-click the left mouse button at the specified coordinates.
* `type`: Type a string of text.
* `screenshot`: Take a screenshot of the screen.
* `wait`: Wait for a specified number of seconds.
* `scroll`: Scroll up, down, left, or right at the specified coordinates.
* `key`: Press a specific keyboard key.
* `left_click_drag`: Drag from start_coordinate to coordinate.
* `zoom`: Take a screenshot of a specific region for closer inspection.
* `scroll_to`: Scroll an element into view using its element reference ID from read_page or find tools.
* `hover`: Move the mouse cursor to the specified coordinates or element without clicking. Useful for revealing tooltips, dropdown menus, or triggering hover states.

coordinate.description: (x, y): The x (pixels from the left edge) and y (pixels from the top edge) coordinates. Required for `left_click`, `right_click`, `double_click`, `triple_click`, and `scroll`. For `left_click_drag`, this is the end position.

text.description: The text to type (for `type` action) or the key(s) to press (for `key` action). For `key` action: Provide space-separated keys (e.g., "Backspace Backspace Delete"). Supports keyboard shortcuts using the platform's modifier key (use "cmd" on Mac, "ctrl" on Windows/Linux, e.g., "cmd+a" or "ctrl+a" for select all). Page zoom shortcuts (e.g. "cmd+=", "ctrl+-", "cmd+0") are not supported - use the `zoom` action to magnify a region of the page instead.

duration.description: The number of seconds to wait. Required for `wait`. Maximum 10 seconds.

scroll_direction.description: The direction to scroll. Required for `scroll`.

scroll_amount.description: The number of scroll wheel ticks. Optional for `scroll`, defaults to 3.

region.description: (x0, y0, x1, y1): The rectangular region to capture for `zoom`. Coordinates define a rectangle from top-left (x0, y0) to bottom-right (x1, y1) in pixels from the viewport origin. Required for `zoom` action. Useful for inspecting small UI elements like icons, buttons, or text.

scale.description: For `screenshot` and `zoom` only. Scale factor in [0.1, 1] for the returned image; 1 (default) uses the full image token budget, 0.5 returns an image at half the width and height (~quarter of the tokens). Coordinates are ALWAYS in the full-resolution coordinate frame (reported with every scaled screenshot), never in the scaled image's own pixels.

repeat.description: Number of times to repeat the key sequence. Only applicable for `key` action. Must be a positive integer between 1 and 100. Default is 1. Useful for navigation tasks like pressing arrow keys multiple times.

ref.description: Element reference ID from read_page or find tools (e.g., "ref_1", "ref_2"). Required for `scroll_to` action. Can be used as alternative to `coordinate` for click actions.

modifiers.description: Modifier keys for click actions. Supports: "ctrl", "shift", "alt", "cmd" (or "meta"), "win" (or "windows"). Can be combined with "+" (e.g., "ctrl+shift", "cmd+alt"). Optional.

tools.description: Emulate a viewport size in the Browser pane tab. Presets: mobile (375x812), tablet (768x1024), or desktop, which clears the size emulation and returns the tab to the pane's own responsive size. Custom sizes need both width and height. An emulated size applies to that tab across reloads and navigation (scaled down to fit when it is larger than the pane): reset it with preset "desktop" as soon as you finish testing. The desktop app may also clear a size you set when your turn ends, so set it again in a later turn if you still need it. A size the user picked from the pane's own Viewport menu is theirs and stays until they or you change it; leave it unless they ask. colorScheme (light/dark) emulates prefers-color-scheme on that tab; it survives reloads and preset "desktop" does not touch it, but the pane re-syncs the tab to the app's light/dark theme when that theme changes or the pane reopens; local documents and static HTML previews always render light. The mobile preset (and any width < 768) also emulates a mobile device: Android Chrome user agent and 5 touch points, so pages detect a touch phone; your clicks still arrive as mouse clicks. Reload the page after switching so load-time device gates re-run.

// swift-tools-version:5.9
import PackageDescription

let package = Package(
    name: "AlmanacCore",
    platforms: [.iOS(.v17), .macOS(.v14)],
    products: [
        .library(name: "AlmanacCore", targets: ["AlmanacCore"])
    ],
    targets: [
        // Vendored SQLite amalgamation (public domain).
        // Vendored rather than system-linked so the Linux core and the iOS app
        // compile against a byte-identical SQLite. Swap for a systemLibrary
        // target if you decide the iOS app should link the OS copy instead.
        .target(
            name: "CSQLite",
            path: "Sources/CSQLite",
            sources: ["sqlite3.c"],
            publicHeadersPath: "include",
            cSettings: [
                .define("SQLITE_ENABLE_FTS5"),
                .define("SQLITE_ENABLE_JSON1"),
                .define("SQLITE_DQS", to: "0"),
                .define("SQLITE_DEFAULT_FOREIGN_KEYS", to: "1"),
                .define("SQLITE_THREADSAFE", to: "1"),
                .define("SQLITE_OMIT_DEPRECATED")
            ]
        ),
        .target(name: "AlmanacCore", dependencies: ["CSQLite"], path: "Sources/AlmanacCore"),
        .testTarget(name: "AlmanacCoreTests", dependencies: ["AlmanacCore"], path: "Tests/AlmanacCoreTests")
    ]
)

// swift-tools-version:5.9
import PackageDescription

let package = Package(
    name: "AlmanacCore",
    platforms: [.iOS(.v17), .macOS(.v14)],
    products: [
        .library(name: "AlmanacCore", targets: ["AlmanacCore"])
    ],
    targets: [
        // Vendored SQLite amalgamation (public domain).
        // Vendored rather than system-linked so the Linux core and the iOS app
        // compile against a byte-identical SQLite. Swap for a systemLibrary
        // target if you decide the iOS app should link the OS copy instead.
        .target(
            name: "CSQLite",
            path: "Sources/CSQLite",
            sources: ["sqlite3.c"],
            publicHeadersPath: "include",
            cSettings: [
                .define("SQLITE_ENABLE_FTS5"),
                .define("SQLITE_ENABLE_JSON1"),
                .define("SQLITE_DQS", to: "0"),
                .define("SQLITE_DEFAULT_FOREIGN_KEYS", to: "1"),
                .define("SQLITE_THREADSAFE", to: "1"),
                .define("SQLITE_OMIT_DEPRECATED")
            ]
        ),
        .target(name: "AlmanacCore", dependencies: ["CSQLite"], path: "Sources/AlmanacCore"),
        .testTarget(name: "AlmanacCoreTests", dependencies: ["AlmanacCore"], path: "Tests/AlmanacCoreTests")
    ]
)

     3	/// Processing Design v0.1 §3 — namespace, never renumber.
     4	///
     5	/// `usda:1105904`, `ciqual:1000`, `cofid:13-145`, `afcd:F002258`.
     6	/// An Almanac-internal integer key is a private detail that must never replace
     7	/// the publisher's identifier. Namespacing keeps a food traceable to its
     8	/// publisher, lets two sources sit side by side, and — the point that matters —
     9	/// keeps "remove a whole source" a one-line delete when a rights holder says no.
    10	public struct SourceIdentifier: Codable, Sendable, Hashable, CustomStringConvertible {
    11	    public let namespace: Namespace
    12	    public let localID: String
    13	
    14	    public enum Namespace: String, Codable, Sendable, CaseIterable, Hashable {
    15	        case usda, ciqual, cofid, afcd, frida
    16	        case openFoodFacts = "off"
    17	        case sfda, wger, freeExerciseDB = "fedb", everkinetic, opentraining
    18	        /// Rows Almanac owns outright. The only namespace Almanac may license
    19	        /// independently.
    20	        case almanac
    21	
    22	        public var licenceGroup: LicenceGroup {
    23	            switch self {
    24	            case .usda, .almanac: return .permissive
    25	            case .ciqual, .cofid, .afcd, .frida: return .attribution
    26	            case .openFoodFacts: return .shareAlike
    27	            case .sfda: return .restricted
    28	            // Exercise sources carry per-entry licences (wger admits ODbL as a
    29	            // possible value). They are never classified at source level —
    30	            // exercise rows must carry their own group column.
    31	            case .wger, .freeExerciseDB, .everkinetic, .opentraining: return .restricted
    32	            }
    33	        }
    34	    }

    36	    public init(namespace: Namespace, localID: String) {
    37	        self.namespace = namespace
    38	        self.localID = localID
    39	    }

    41	    public var description: String { "\(namespace.rawValue):\(localID)" }

    43	    public init?(parsing text: String) {
    44	        guard let sep = text.firstIndex(of: ":") else { return nil }

     1	import Foundation
     2	
     3	/// One forward schema change. Migrations are append-only and never edited
     4	/// once they have run on a device — that is the whole contract.
     5	public protocol Migration: Sendable {
     6	    /// Strictly increasing, unique, never reused.
     7	    static var version: Int { get }
     8	    /// Human label recorded in `schema_migrations` for forensics.
     9	    static var name: String { get }
    10	    static func up(_ db: Database) throws
    11	}
    12	
    13	public struct AppliedMigration: Sendable, Hashable {
    14	    public let version: Int
    15	    public let name: String
    16	    public let appliedAt: Date
    17	}
    18	
    19	public enum MigrationError: Error, CustomStringConvertible, Sendable {
    20	    case duplicateVersion(Int)
    21	    case outOfOrder(applied: Int, pending: Int)
    22	    case checksumDrift(version: Int, storedName: String, incomingName: String)
    23	
    24	    public var description: String {
    25	        switch self {
    26	        case .duplicateVersion(let v):
    27	            return "Two migrations declare version \(v). Versions must be unique."
    28	        case .outOfOrder(let applied, let pending):
    29	            return """
    30	            Migration \(pending) is older than \(applied), which is already applied. \
    31	            A migration inserted behind the head would run on new installs but never \
    32	            on existing ones. Give it a version above \(applied).
    33	            """
    34	        case .checksumDrift(let v, let stored, let incoming):
    35	            return """
    36	            Migration \(v) ran as "\(stored)" but is now declared as "\(incoming)". \
    37	            An applied migration must never be edited — add a new one instead.

    40	    }

     1	import Foundation
     2	
     3	/// Applies pending migrations in version order, each in its own transaction.
     4	///
     5	/// Three guarantees, in order of how expensive they are to lose:
     6	///  1. A migration that throws leaves the database exactly as it was.
     7	///  2. A migration already applied never runs twice.
     8	///  3. Editing an applied migration is detected and refused, rather than
     9	///     silently producing two different schemas in the field.
    10	public struct MigrationRunner: Sendable {
    11	    private let migrations: [any Migration.Type]
    12	    private let clock: any Clock
    13	
    14	    public init(migrations: [any Migration.Type], clock: any Clock = SystemClock()) throws {
    15	        var seen = Set<Int>()
    16	        for m in migrations {
    17	            guard seen.insert(m.version).inserted else {
    18	                throw MigrationError.duplicateVersion(m.version)
    19	            }
    20	        }
    21	        self.migrations = migrations.sorted { $0.version < $1.version }
    22	        self.clock = clock
    23	    }
    24	
    25	    private static let bootstrap = """
    26	    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS schema_migrations (
    27	        version     INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    28	        name        TEXT    NOT NULL,
    29	        applied_at  TEXT    NOT NULL
    30	    );
    31	    """
    32	
    33	    public func applied(in db: Database) throws -> [AppliedMigration] {
    34	        try db.execute(Self.bootstrap)
    35	        let rows = try db.query("SELECT version, name, applied_at FROM schema_migrations ORDER BY version;")
    36	        return rows.compactMap { row in
    37	            guard let v = row.int("version"),
    38	                  let n = row.string("name"),
    39	                  let t = row.string("applied_at"),
    40	                  let d = ISO8601DateFormatter().date(from: t) else { return nil }
    41	            return AppliedMigration(version: Int(v), name: n, appliedAt: d)
    42	        }
    43	    }
    44	
    45	    /// Returns the versions actually applied by this call.
    46	    @discardableResult
    47	    public func migrate(_ db: Database) throws -> [Int] {
    48	        let already = try applied(in: db)
    49	        let appliedByVersion = Dictionary(uniqueKeysWithValues: already.map { ($0.version, $0.name) })
    50	        let head = already.map(\.version).max() ?? 0
    51	
    52	        for m in migrations {
    53	            if let storedName = appliedByVersion[m.version], storedName != m.name {
    54	                throw MigrationError.checksumDrift(
    55	                    version: m.version, storedName: storedName, incomingName: m.name
    56	                )
    57	            }
    58	            if appliedByVersion[m.version] == nil && m.version < head {
    59	                throw MigrationError.outOfOrder(applied: head, pending: m.version)
    60	            }
    61	        }
    62	
    63	        var ran: [Int] = []
    64	        for m in migrations where appliedByVersion[m.version] == nil {
    65	            try db.transaction {
    66	                try m.up(db)
    67	                try db.run(
    68	                    "INSERT INTO schema_migrations (version, name, applied_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?);",
    69	                    [.integer(Int64(m.version)),
    70	                     .text(m.name),
    71	                     .text(ISO8601DateFormatter().string(from: clock.now))]
    72	                )
    73	            }
    74	            ran.append(m.version)
    75	        }
    76	        return ran
    77	    }
    78	}

     5	public protocol Migration: Sendable {

    21	    case outOfOrder(applied: Int, pending: Int)
    22	    case checksumDrift(version: Int, storedName: String, incomingName: String)

    34	        case .checksumDrift(let v, let stored, let incoming):

     1	import Foundation
     2	
     3	/// Applies pending migrations in version order, each in its own transaction.
     4	///
     5	/// Three guarantees, in order of how expensive they are to lose:
     6	///  1. A migration that throws leaves the database exactly as it was.
     7	///  2. A migration already applied never runs twice.
     8	///  3. Editing an applied migration is detected and refused, rather than
     9	///     silently producing two different schemas in the field.
    10	public struct MigrationRunner: Sendable {
    11	    private let migrations: [any Migration.Type]
    12	    private let clock: any Clock
    13	
    14	    public init(migrations: [any Migration.Type], clock: any Clock = SystemClock()) throws {
    15	        var seen = Set<Int>()
    16	        for m in migrations {
    17	            guard seen.insert(m.version).inserted else {
    18	                throw MigrationError.duplicateVersion(m.version)
    19	            }
    20	        }
    21	        self.migrations = migrations.sorted { $0.version < $1.version }
    22	        self.clock = clock
    23	    }
    24	
    25	    private static let bootstrap = """
    26	    CREATE TABLE IF NOT EXISTS schema_migrations (
    27	        version     INTEGER PRIMARY KEY,
    28	        name        TEXT    NOT NULL,
    29	        applied_at  TEXT    NOT NULL
    30	    );
    31	    """
    32	
    33	    public func applied(in db: Database) throws -> [AppliedMigration] {
    34	        try db.execute(Self.bootstrap)
    35	        let rows = try db.query("SELECT version, name, applied_at FROM schema_migrations ORDER BY version;")
    36	        return rows.compactMap { row in
    37	            guard let v = row.int("version"),
    38	                  let n = row.string("name"),
    39	                  let t = row.string("applied_at"),
    40	                  let d = ISO8601DateFormatter().date(from: t) else { return nil }
    41	            return AppliedMigration(version: Int(v), name: n, appliedAt: d)
    42	        }
    43	    }
    44	
    45	    /// Returns the versions actually applied by this call.
    46	    @discardableResult
    47	    public func migrate(_ db: Database) throws -> [Int] {
    48	        let already = try applied(in: db)
    49	        let appliedByVersion = Dictionary(uniqueKeysWithValues: already.map { ($0.version, $0.name) })
    50	        let head = already.map(\.version).max() ?? 0
    51	
    52	        for m in migrations {
    53	            if let storedName = appliedByVersion[m.version], storedName != m.name {
    54	                throw MigrationError.checksumDrift(
    55	                    version: m.version, storedName: storedName, incomingName: m.name
    56	                )
    57	            }
    58	            if appliedByVersion[m.version] == nil && m.version < head {
    59	                throw MigrationError.outOfOrder(applied: head, pending: m.version)
    60	            }
    61	        }
    62	
    63	        var ran: [Int] = []
    64	        for m in migrations where appliedByVersion[m.version] == nil {
    65	            try db.transaction {
    66	                try m.up(db)
    67	                try db.run(
    68	                    "INSERT INTO schema_migrations (version, name, applied_at) VALUES (?, ?, ?);",
    69	                    [.integer(Int64(m.version)),
    70	                     .text(m.name),
    71	                     .text(ISO8601DateFormatter().string(from: clock.now))]
    72	                )
    73	            }
    74	            ran.append(m.version)
    75	        }
    76	        return ran
    77	    }
    78	}

    79	2. **Prescribed versus achieved.** Prescription Model §1-2, and the
    80	   order-versus-result split in Laboratory.
    81	3. **Source identifier plus a mapping held as data.** Nutrient dictionary
    82	   (Processing Design §6), prescription map (Prescription Model §6), analyte
    83	   catalog (Laboratory §4.5). Three instances of one construct.
    84	4. **Licence classification of shipped reference data.** Already implemented.
    85	5. **Day assignment.** Every module; one rule; already implemented in `TimeModel`.
    86	6. **Time precision and zone.** §8 — newly recognised as shared in v0.2.
    87	7. **Import jobs and sync cursors.** §9 — newly separated in v0.2.
    88	8. **Identity and external references.** §10 — newly recognised as shared.
    89	9. **Units with an explicit basis.** Per-100 g versus per-100 mL (Processing
    90	   Design §4) and lab unit classes (Laboratory §8).
    91	
    92	---
    93	
    94	## 4. What stays specific to each module
    95	
    96	- **Nutrition** — nutrient dictionary, portion and gram-weight conversion,
    97	  per-100 g versus per-100 mL basis, and the refusal to deduplicate foods
    98	  across sources (Processing Design §6).
    99	- **Exercise** — twelve prescription types × ten containers, per-type
   100	  progression axes including two that move in opposite directions on the same
   101	  clock, and readiness coupling (Prescription Model §2-5). A bout's *measured
   102	  field* is determined by its type.
   103	- **Laboratory** — catalog and aliases, panels, reports, source documents,
   104	  reference ranges as printed, revision chains, and the five value dimensions.
   105	- **Sleep and device samples** — interval semantics with overlapping stages,
   106	  device provenance, deletion by external identifier.
   107	
   108	None of these generalise. The foundation's job is to serve them, not to
   109	absorb them.
   110	
   111	---
   112	
   113	## 5. Events, measurements, plans, derived summaries
   114	
   115	| | Definition | Mutability | Example |
   116	|---|---|---|---|
   117	| **Event** | Something that happened at a time or over an interval. | Correctable by revision, never silently overwritten. | A specimen collected; a bout performed; a meal eaten. |
   118	| **Measurement** | A qualified value attached to an event or subject. | Append-only; an amendment is a new revision. | A ferritin observation; a nutrient amount; an HR sample. |
   119	| **Plan** | A prescribed intention that may or may not be executed. | Has its own lifecycle. | An ordered panel; a prescribed 5×5; a protein target. |
   120	| **Derived summary** | Computed by a versioned rule from the above. | Droppable and rebuildable. | Daily macro totals; a readiness score; an eGFR Almanac computed. |
   121	
   122	Three rules, each with direct evidence:
   123	
   124	1. **A plan is never stored in the same row as its outcome** — Prescription
   125	   Model §1. An ordered panel that returned "insufficient specimen" is a plan
   126	   with no measurement and must stay visible as exactly that.
   127	2. **A measurement is never stored without its qualifying dimensions and its
   128	   preserved source text** — Processing Design §2; Laboratory §5.
   129	3. **A derived summary records the rule version and its inputs, and is never
   130	   the only copy of a fact** — Laboratory §6.2 is the concrete instance.
   131	
   132	---
   133	
   134	## 6. Shared measurement storage versus shared interfaces
   135	
   136	v0.1 said a shared measurement model is information-destroying. That was
   137	wrong, and §13 records the correction. A shared model with enough dimensions —
   138	value type, comparator, derivation, missing reason, source text, unit class,
   139	precision — destroys nothing. What destroys information is an *under-specified*
   140	shared model: a bare `value REAL` with an untyped `metadata JSON` beside it.
   141	
   142	So the real question is not "shared or specialised" but **what would a shared
   143	model have to carry, and what does it cost to make every module pay for it.**
   144	
   145	| | One shared measurement table | Per-module tables |
   146	|---|---|---|
   147	| Dimensions | Must be the union of every module's: lab's five plus comparator plus ranges plus revision chain, nutrition's qualifier plus basis, exercise's type-dependent measured field. | Each module carries only its own. |
   148	| Constraints | Table-level constraints must hold for every module, so most become nullable and unenforced; per-module validity moves into application code. | `CHECK` and `NOT NULL` express each module's real rules. |
   149	| Foreign keys | Cannot point at module-specific parents (specimen, meal, bout) from one table without polymorphism. | Direct and enforced. |
   150	| Aggregation | No shared aggregation is meaningful across modules anyway; every query re-adds module knowledge in its predicates. | Each module aggregates its own. |
   151	| Schema change | A new module's dimension widens the shared table for all modules and rewrites one large table. | Additive, isolated. |
   152	| Cross-module queries | Single table scan. | Requires a union or per-module queries. |
   153	| Migration cost if reversed | Splitting a populated shared table per module is a data migration. | Merging later is also a data migration. |
   154	
   155	The deciding factor is not information loss. It is that the union of
   156	dimensions is large, mostly nullable outside its own module, and unenforceable
   157	at the table level — and the only benefit, one-table cross-module querying, is
   158	addressed by §7 without a shared payload table.
   159	
   160	**Chosen: per-module tables, with shared behaviour expressed as protocols.**
   161	
   162	---
   163	
   164	## 7. The timeline — reassessment
   165	
   166	v0.1 proposed a persisted `health_event` index. This section reconsiders it
   167	against the alternative of module-provided queries.
   168	
   169	**Module-provided queries:** each module implements a protocol returning its
   170	own entries for a time range from its own tables; a thin coordinator merges the
   171	results and orders them. No shared table, no second copy of anything.
   172	
   173	**Persisted event index:** each module also writes a row into a shared index
   174	table; the coordinator queries that one table.
   175	
   176	| | Module-provided queries | Persisted event index |
   177	|---|---|---|
   178	| Second copy of data | None. | Yes — index rows duplicate identity and time. |
   179	| Consistency risk | None. The module's record is the only copy. | Dual write; index can drift on insert, update, delete or revision. |
   180	| Cross-module day view | N queries, merged in memory. | One indexed query. |
   181	| Paging across long history | Needs an N-way merge cursor. | Natural. |
   182	| Deletions and revisions | Automatic — the record is the truth. | Needs cascade rules and orphan repair. |
   183	| New shared table names | None. | Occupies a generic name the unavailable spec may want (§12). |
   184	| Cost to introduce later | Additive; buildable from module records at any time. | — |
   185	| Cost to remove later | — | Modules already write to it; removal is a migration. |
   186	
   187	**Chosen: module-provided queries. The index is deferred.**
   188	
   189	*Implemented in exactly this form:* `TimelineProviding` on `LabStore` and
   190	`HealthSampleStore`, merged by `Timeline` with a total order, and **no index
   191	table**. See `docs/implementation-status.md` §2C.
   192	
   193	The concrete reason: the index's only genuine advantage is query performance
   194	and paging ergonomics, and **there is no performance problem to solve** —
   195	there are no modules, no data, no UI, and no measurement showing that an
   196	N-way merge is too slow. Every other row favours the queries, and the
   197	asymmetry is decisive: the index can be added later from module records
   198	without changing a single module table, whereas removing it after modules
   199	write to it is a data migration. Choosing the reversible option costs nothing
   200	today.
   201	
   202	The trigger for revisiting, stated so the deferral is not indefinite: when a
   203	range view must merge more than four modules, or page across more than a year
   204	of history, **and** profiling shows the merge dominating.
   205	
   206	### 7.1 The protocol
   207	
   208	```swift
   209	public protocol TimelineProviding {
   210	    static var domain: String { get }
   211	    func entries(from: Date, to: Date, in db: Database) throws -> [TimelineEntry]
   212	}
   213	
   214	public struct TimelineEntry: Sendable {
   215	    public let domain: String
   216	    public let kind: String
   217	    public let recordTable: String
   218	    public let recordID: String
   219	    public let occurrence: OccurrenceTime      // §8 — precision and zone
   220	    public let title: String
   221	    public let detail: String?
   222	    public let value: ValuePresentation
   223	    public let lifecycle: String               // module's own vocabulary
   224	}
   225	
   226	public enum ValuePresentation: Sendable {
   227	    case none
   228	    case quantity(text: String, unit: String?)
   229	    case bounded(comparator: String, text: String, unit: String?)
   230	    case coded(text: String)
   231	    case narrative(text: String)
   232	    case ratio(text: String)
   233	    case titer(text: String)
   234	    case missing(reason: String)
   235	    case derived(text: String, ruleVersion: String)
   236	}
   237	```
   238	
   239	v0.1's `isEstimated: Bool` is removed. Missing, qualitative and bounded values
   240	are three different things and each has its own case; the module formats its
   241	own value and the timeline never reinterprets it.
   242	
   243	### 7.2 If the index is later adopted
   244	
   245	Requirements, so that the deferral does not become a trap:
   246	
   247	- **Fully rebuildable from domain records alone.** A maintenance routine must
   248	  be able to drop the table and repopulate it entirely from module data.
   249	- **Update, delete and revision coverage.** Each module exposes a
   250	  `changes(since:)` contract; the index is not maintained by hand-written
   251	  call sites.
   252	- **Orphan repair.** An index row whose target no longer exists is detected
   253	  and removed by a routine, not by a foreign key — SQLite cannot enforce one
   254	  against a polymorphic target.
   255	- **Staleness detection.** The table records the schema version and the day
   256	  boundary tag it was built under, so a boundary change or a schema change is
   257	  detectable rather than silent.
   258	- **A derived artefact, never a source.** Losing the index must never lose a
   259	  fact.
   260	
   261	---
   262	
   263	## 8. Time, precision and zone
   264	
   265	Shared across every module. Laboratory §12 is the module-specific application.
   266	
   267	- Four distinct times, never interchangeable: **scheduled** (a plan's intended
   268	  time), **occurrence** (when the thing happened — collection, meal, bout,
   269	  sleep segment), **recording** (when it entered Almanac), and where a source
   270	  issues records, **reported** (when the source issued it).
   271	- Every stored time carries a **precision**: `instant` · `minute` · `hour` ·
   272	  `day` · `month` · `year` · `unknown`.
   273	- Every stored time carries an offset and, where known, a zone identifier, so
   274	  a record made in another zone is not reinterpreted in the device's current
   275	  one.
   276	- **No timestamp is ever fabricated to fill a field.** A date-only fact stays
   277	  at `day` precision.
   278	
   279	Day assignment:
   280	
   281	- Uses the occurrence time where present, else the reported time, else the
   282	  recording time, and **records which was used**.
   283	- Goes through `TimeModel` (`Time/TimeModel.swift`); no module formats a date.
   284	- At `day` precision or coarser with a non-midnight boundary, the assignment
   285	  is marked approximate. The boundary is still a placeholder
   286	  (`TimeModel.swift:16-20`), so this case is currently the common one and must
   287	  not be resolved by assuming a time.
   288	
   289	Interval overlap:
   290	
   291	- Defined only when both intervals have known start and end at `minute`
   292	  precision or finer with known offsets.
   293	- Otherwise the answer is **unknown**, which is a third value and not `false`.
   294	  Sleep stage overlap, fasting windows and workout merging all depend on this.
   295	
   296	Ordering:
   297	
   298	- Records at `minute` precision or finer order against each other.
   299	- Coarser records group as time-unknown within their day rather than sorting
   300	  against an invented time.
   301	
   302	---
   303	
   304	## 9. Import jobs and synchronisation cursors
   305	
   306	v0.1 conflated these. They are different mechanisms with different failure
   307	modes.
   308	
   309	| | Import job | Sync cursor |
   310	|---|---|---|
   311	| Input | A document or file the user supplied. | A change stream the source exposes. |
   312	| Identity | The document. | The stream position. |
   313	| Progress record | Job row: status, counts, per-row outcomes, errors, document link. | Opaque anchor token per domain. |
   314	| Re-running | Idempotent by source identity; produces the same rows. | Resumes from the anchor. |
   315	| Failure | The job fails; the document remains; nothing is lost. | The anchor must not advance past unpersisted data. |
   316	| Existing code | None. | `Sync/SyncAnchorStore.swift`, `sync_anchor` table. |
   317	
   318	Two requirements follow.
   319	
   320	- **R9.1** File imports get their own job record. They do not use
   321	  `sync_anchor`, and a cursor is not invented for them.
   322	- **R9.2** For incremental sync, **the imported records and the cursor advance
   323	  commit in one transaction.** Today `SyncAnchorStore.save` is an independent
   324	  call (`Sync/SyncAnchorStore.swift:44`), so advancing the anchor without
   325	  persisting the rows it covers is expressible — and if it happened, the next
   326	  sync would start after data that was never stored, skipping it permanently.
   327	  `Database.transaction` (`Database.swift:168-178`) already supports the fix;
   328	  what is needed is an API shape that takes the row-writing work and the
   329	  advance together, so the unsafe ordering cannot be written.
   330	
   331	  This is a required interface change to `SyncAnchorStore`. It is **not made in
   332	  this revision** — no application code has been changed. The stored schema
   333	  does not change; only the call shape does.
   334	
   335	- **R9.3** `recordFailure` keeps its current behaviour: a failure never clears
   336	  the last good anchor (`:59-67`).
   337	
   338	---
   339	
   340	## 10. Identity and external references
   341	
   342	Shared rules; Laboratory §9 is the module-specific application.
   343	
   344	- **R10.1** Every record has an Almanac-owned surrogate identifier. No natural
   345	  key serves as primary identity.
   346	- **R10.2** External identifiers are **scoped to their issuing source**.
   347	  Uniqueness applies to `(source_system, external_id)`, never to `external_id`
   348	  alone. Two sources may legitimately use the same string.
   349	- **R10.3** Repeated observations of the same thing are preserved as distinct
   350	  records. Nothing is deduplicated on the assumption that a repeat is an error.
   351	- **R10.4** Revisions form a chain: a new record referencing the one it
   352	  replaces, with a reason. The replaced record is retained and marked
   353	  superseded. Nothing is overwritten in place.
   354	- **R10.5** When idempotency cannot be established, the import creates a new
   355	  record and marks it as a possible duplicate for review. Silent merging is
   356	  prohibited.
   357	
   358	This applies equally to HealthKit samples: `HealthChangeSet.deletedExternalIDs`
   359	(`Health/HealthProvider.swift:48`) deletes by external identifier, and that
   360	deletion must be scoped to the providing source.
   361	
   362	---
   363	
   364	## 11. Migration numbering
   365	
   366	### 11.1 What is actually applied
   367	
   368	Nothing. Per §1: one migration is *declared* (version 1, `core_infrastructure`),
   369	and no durable database exists in the repository, in `.build/`, or at any path
   370	configured in source. Tests build in-memory or UUID-named temporary databases.
   371	
   372	Consequences:
   373	
   374	- **Preserving applied migrations is satisfied trivially** — there are none.
   375	- **Migration 001 is preserved as declared anyway.** Its version and `name`
   376	  stay exactly as they are. It is referenced by `AlmanacMigrations.all`
   377	  (`Migrations.swift:50-56`), by the tests, and by `README.md`; changing it
   378	  buys nothing and would invalidate the runner's drift check the moment a
   379	  database exists.
   380	- **Numbering is not yet frozen, and freezes the moment an app target creates
   381	  its first durable database.** That is the deadline, and it is worth writing
   382	  down because it will arrive without an announcement.
   383	
   384	### 11.2 The sequence
   385	
   386	| | Number new work 002 upward now | Reserve a block for the spec's schema |
   387	|---|---|---|
   388	| Requires knowing how many migrations the spec needs | No | Yes — which is inference about an unavailable document |
   389	| If the spec's schema must land first | Renumber the not-yet-applied local migrations, free while nothing is applied | No renumber |
   390	| If the reserved block is the wrong size | — | Either wasted numbers or the same renumber anyway |
   391	| Risk after the first durable database exists | Renumber is no longer free; the fix becomes a new higher migration | Same |
   392	
   393	**Recommended sequence:** keep `001 core_infrastructure` unchanged; number new
   394	module migrations `002` upward contiguously as they are authored; and treat
   395	renumbering as available until the first durable database is created. Record
   396	the freeze point in `README.md` when the app target lands.
   397	
   398	*Taken:* migration 001 `core_infrastructure` unchanged; 002
   399	`laboratory_catalog`, 003 `laboratory_records`, 004 `health_samples`. The
   400	target-database check that preceded this, and how far its evidence reaches,
   401	is recorded in `docs/implementation-status.md` §4.
   402	
   403	### 11.3 Correcting v0.1 on recoverability
   404	
   405	v0.1 said applying a migration above the spec's reserved number would make
   406	that number "unrecoverable". That is wrong. `MigrationError.outOfOrder`
   407	(`MigrationRunner.swift:58-60`) is a policy in code, and the situation has at
   408	least three exits: renumber the pending migration above the applied head; ship
   409	the same schema change as a new higher-numbered migration; or, before any
   410	release, reset development databases. The real costs are narrower and worth
   411	stating accurately — installs that applied different orders can diverge, and
   412	after field installs a correction must be a new migration rather than an edit.
   413	
   414	---
   415	
   416	## 12. Does the missing Technical Spec create schema conflicts beyond numbering?
   417	
   418	Yes — three, all semantic rather than mechanical. None of them is a numbering
   419	problem, and numbering is the least of them.
   420	
   421	1. **Duplicate definition of the same concept.** If the spec's 48 tables
   422	   already define laboratory, sleep or timeline structures, building them now
   423	   creates two homes for one fact. Reconciling that later is a data migration,
   424	   not a rename.
   425	2. **Name occupation.** A 48-table schema plausibly wants generic names —
   426	   `event`, `observation`, `measurement`, `sample`, `source`, `document`. Any
   427	   taken now forces the transcription to rename as it goes, and renaming
   428	   during transcription is exactly where transcription errors enter.
   429	3. **Contradicting invariants.** The spec defines the day-boundary rule, the
   430	   readiness definition and the workout merge model. A module that hard-codes
   431	   an assumption about any of them will disagree with the transcription
   432	   silently rather than loudly.
   433	
   434	Mitigations, all cheap and all adopted by this proposal:
   435	
   436	- Prefix every new table with its module (`lab_*`). Claim no generic name.
   437	- Introduce no new shared table at all — which §7 already concluded on other
   438	  grounds, and which removes conflict class 2 for the timeline entirely.
   439	- Hard-code no boundary, readiness or merge assumption; take them from
   440	  injected configuration.
   441	- Keep everything additive, so the transcription adds tables rather than
   442	  reconciling them.
   443	
   444	One scoping observation worth stating: blood-test tracking entered Almanac's
   445	scope on 2026-09-08, and the spec is dated 2026-08-05. It is therefore
   446	**likely, though unverified, that Laboratory is not among the 48 tables** — in
   447	which case conflict class 1 does not apply to this module. That is a
   448	probability, not a finding, and it is listed as an open question in §15.
   449	
   450	---
   451	
   452	## 13. Corrections to v0.1
   453	
   454	| v0.1 said | Correction |
   455	|---|---|
   456	| Only results with matching measured/calculated status are comparable. | Matching derivation status does **not** establish comparability. Analyte identity, method, assay, unit and reference frame must also agree, and often cannot be determined from the report. Almanac surfaces the differences rather than asserting comparability. Laboratory §15.1. |
   457	| Unit conversion is analyte-specific because it needs molar mass. | Only mass↔substance-amount conversion needs molar mass. Decimal scaling within one dimension is general, and dimensionless values need nothing. Laboratory §8. |
   458	| A generic value column is "the coercion promoted to an architecture"; a shared measurement model destroys information. | A sufficiently dimensioned shared model destroys nothing. The objection is to *under-specified* shared storage. Per-module tables are chosen for constraint enforcement, foreign keys and isolated schema change — §6. |
   459	| Applying a migration above the reserved number makes it permanently unapplicable. | The refusal is a recoverable policy. The real costs are divergence between installs and needing a new migration rather than an edit after release. §11.3. |
   460	| Almanac does not interpret results, ever. | Interpretation is deferred for v1, not permanently prohibited. The data model supports adding it, provided interpretation is stored separately from source facts, versioned and attributable. Laboratory §18.2. |
   461	| A single `lab_qualifier` enum. | Five orthogonal dimensions, plus mandatory preserved source text. Laboratory §5. |
   462	| Uniqueness on (lab, report, analyte). | Surrogate identity, source-scoped external identifiers, preserved repeats and revision chains. §10, Laboratory §9. |
   463	| Lab imports use `sync_anchor`. | Import jobs and sync cursors are separate mechanisms. §9. |
   464	| A persisted `health_event` index. | Module-provided timeline queries; index deferred with a stated trigger. §7. |
   465	| `TimelineSummary.isEstimated: Bool`. | Structured `ValuePresentation`; missing, qualitative and bounded are distinct. §7.1. |
   466	
   467	---
   468	
   469	## 14. Verification
   470	
   471	**Nothing below has been run.** The Swift toolchain lives at
   472	`~/.local/swift/` on `yamal`, outside the folder this session can reach, so no
   473	build or test was executed during this revision. The last recorded successful
   474	run is in the 2026-09-05 status note; this revision changed only Markdown under
   475	`docs/`, and `git diff --stat` over tracked files is empty.
   476	
   477	When the module work begins, these are the checks that matter:
   478	
   479	1. **Baseline** — `source env.sh && swift build && swift test` before any code
   480	   change, to establish the current count rather than assume it.
   481	2. **Cursor atomicity** — a sync whose row write throws must leave the anchor
   482	   unmoved, so the next run re-reads the same range. This is §9's R9.2 and is
   483	   the single most consequential test

     2

     4	preserved. Changes are local on `codex/manual-entry`. Nothing pushed.
     5	
     6	## Verified core

     9	Command: `swift test -j 1 -Xswiftc -disable-batch-mode`.

1	# Almanac — Processing Design v0.1
     2	
     3	**Status:** design only. `processed/` is empty and stays empty until a stage
     4	below is deliberately executed.
     5	**Date:** 2026-09-01 · Phase 16 lifted the same day.
     6	**Inputs:** `DATASETS.csv`, `LICENSES.md`, and Technical Specification v1.0
     7	(48-table iOS/SQLite schema, HealthKit sync, provenance enums in Slice 1).
     8	
     9	---
    10	
    11	## 1. The constraint that drives everything else
    12	
    13	Almanac ships as an iOS app with an on-device SQLite database. That single fact
    14	converts the licensing analysis from paperwork into architecture:
    15	
    16	> **Putting a food row in the app bundle is redistributing it to every user who
    17	> installs the app.**
    18	
    19	Not "using" it. Not "referencing" it. Redistributing — to an unbounded audience,
    20	commercially, in a form they keep on their device. This is the strictest
    21	possible reading of every licence in `LICENSES.md`, and it is the correct one.
    22	
    23	Three consequences fall straight out:
    24	
    25	| | Rule |
    26	|---|---|
    27	| **Group A + B** | May ship inside the app bundle. Attribution obligations travel with them. |
    28	| **Group C** (ODbL) | Must **never** enter the bundle. Share-alike would attach to the shipped database itself. |
    29	| **Group D** | Must **never** enter the bundle. Includes all five FAO datasets, SFDA, Bahrain ×2, INNTA, IFCT, NEVO, TBCA. |
    30	
    31	**What actually ships in v1** is therefore already decided, and it is not small:
    32	
    33	| Dataset | Licence | Foods |
    34	|---|---|---:|
    35	| USDA FoodData Central | CC0 1.0 | 2,101,280 |
    36	| ANSES-CIQUAL 2025 | CC BY 4.0 + Etalab 2.0 | 3,484 |
    37	| CoFID 2021 | OGL v3.0 | 2,887 |
    38	| AFCD Release 3 | CC BY 4.0 | 1,588 |
    39	| **Total** | | **~2.11 M** |
    40	
    41	Frida (CC BY 4.0) joins this tier the moment it is downloaded. Nothing here
    42	waits on a single reply to a single email.
    43	
    44	### The trap to design against
    45	The failure mode is not "we ship ODbL data by accident on day one." It is:
    46	someone adds SFDA dishes to make Saudi search work, six months of user data
    47	accumulates against those food IDs, and then the rights answer comes back "no".
    48	At that point the data cannot be removed by deleting rows — user log entries
    49	point at it, and the export the user downloads contains it.
    50	
    51	**So the boundary is enforced structurally, not by discipline.** A licence group
    52	is a column on every food row and a filter on the bundle build, and the build
    53	fails loudly rather than shipping a mixed database.
    54	
    55	---
    56	
    57	## 2. Per-value provenance, because all four sources already have it
    58	
    59	This is the discovery from surveying the files, and it changes the schema.
    60	
    61	Every one of the four clean sources ships quality metadata **per nutrient
    62	value** — in four incompatible vocabularies:
    63	
    64	| Source | What it carries per value |
    65	|---|---|
    66	| **USDA** | `derivation_id`, `data_points`, `min`/`max`/`median`, `loq`, `min_year_acquired` |
    67	| **CIQUAL** | `code_confiance` (A–D confidence), `source_code`, optional `min`/`max` |
    68	| **CoFID** | `Tr` (trace), `N` (not analysed) tokens **in the value cell itself** |
    69	| **AFCD** | `Derivation` column: `Borrowed`, `Recipe`, analysed |
    70	
    71	Concretely, the proximates sheet of CoFID alone carries **4,101 `Tr` and 2,874
    72	`N`** values. The naive pipeline casts those to float, gets `NaN`, and writes
    73	`0` or `NULL`.
    74	
    75	Both are wrong, and wrong in a way that matters to a body-monitor product:
    76	
    77	- `Tr` means *present in trace amounts* — not zero.
    78	- `N` means *nobody measured it* — not zero, and not "absent".
    79	
    80	Rendering "not analysed" as **0 mg of iron** tells a user their intake is zero
    81	when the truth is unknown. That is the single most consequential bug available
    82	in this entire project, and it is introduced by a one-line type coercion.
    83	
    84	### The value model
    85	A nutrient value is therefore never a bare number:
    86	
    87	```
    88	nutrient_value(
    89	  food_ref,            -- namespaced, see §3
    90	  nutrient_id,         -- canonical
    91	  amount              REAL     NULL,   -- NULL only when genuinely unmeasured
    92	  qualifier           TEXT     NOT NULL,
    93	  confidence          TEXT     NULL,   -- source's own grade, verbatim
    94	  source_value        TEXT     NOT NULL,-- the original cell, unparsed
    95	  source_nutrient_id  TEXT     NOT NULL,
    96	  source_unit         TEXT     NOT NULL,
    97	  licence_group       CHAR(1)  NOT NULL
    98	)
    99	```
   100	
   101	`qualifier` is a closed enum — the spec's Slice 1 already calls for provenance
   102	enums, so this lands in existing plans:
   103	
   104	`measured` · `trace` · `not_analysed` · `below_loq` · `borrowed` ·
   105	`calculated_recipe` · `calculated_factor` · `zero_reported`
   106	
   107	Note `zero_reported` is distinct from `trace` and from `not_analysed`. Three
   108	different facts that a float column collapses into one.
   109	
   110	`source_value` is the reversibility guarantee: whatever the parser gets wrong,
   111	the original cell is still there to re-derive from without returning to `raw/`.
   112	
   113	---
   114	
   115	## 3. Identifiers — namespace, never renumber
   116	
   117	```
   118	usda:1105904      ciqual:1000      cofid:13-145      afcd:F002258
   119	```
   120	
   121	Source identifiers are stable, published, and cited in the literature. An
   122	Almanac-internal integer key is a private detail that must never replace them.
   123	Namespacing costs a few bytes and buys three things: a food is always traceable
   124	to its publisher, two sources can be held side by side without collision, and
   125	**removing a whole source stays a one-line delete** — which is exactly what a
   126	"no" from a rights holder will require.
   127	
   128	Almanac-native records get their own namespace, `almanac:`, and are the only
   129	rows Almanac owns outright (per `LICENSES.md`, "What Almanac may license
   130	independently").
   131	
   132	---
   133	
   134	## 4. Units — two traps
   135	
   136	**Trap 1: per 100 g vs per 100 mL.** AFCD ships these as *separate sheets*
   137	(`All solids & liquids per 100 g`, `Liquids only per 100 mL`) because they are
   138	not interchangeable. Merging them into one `per_100` column silently corrupts
   139	every liquid. The basis is a column, not an assumption.
   140	
   141	**Trap 2: the density database is Group D.** Converting household measures
   142	("1 cup") to mass is core to the product, and the obvious tool — the FAO/INFOODS
   143	Density Database, 6,565 records — carries *"all rights reserved"* with no
   144	standing grant. It cannot ship.
   145	
   146	The workable substitute is already in hand and is CC0: USDA's `food_portion`
   147	table maps `fdc_id` + `measure_unit` → `gram_weight` directly, with 47,446 rows,
   148	and CoFID carries `Specific gravity` and `Edible proportion` per food under OGL.
   149	Portion conversion is therefore solved for Group A/B without FAO — worth knowing
   150	before anyone budgets a licence fee for it.
   151	
   152	---
   153	
   154	## 5. Pipeline stages
   155	
   156	Each stage is a separate directory. No stage overwrites its input, and the merge
   157	step is deliberately the *last* one.
   158	
   159	```
   160	raw/                 immutable, 0444, already verified
   161	  ↓  extract         per source, no merging, no renaming
   162	processed/extracted/{source}/     source's own shape, machine-readable
   163	  ↓  canonicalise    per source, STILL SEPARATE
   164	processed/canonical/{source}/     Almanac schema, source values preserved
   165	  ↓  union           licence-filtered, group column enforced
   166	processed/union/                  one queryable set, all groups tagged
   167	  ↓  bundle          Group A+B only, hard-failing filter
   168	build/almanac.sqlite              what actually ships
   169	```
   170	
   171	The property worth protecting: **you can delete any single `canonical/{source}/`
   172	directory and rebuild** without touching anything else. That is what makes a
   173	"no" from FAO or SFDA survivable.
   174	
   175	`processed/union/` may contain Group C and D — it is a local research artefact,
   176	never a shipped one. Only the bundle step filters, and it filters by asserting,
   177	not by hoping:
   178	
   179	```
   180	assert every row's licence_group in ('A','B') else FAIL THE BUILD
   181	```
   182	
   183	---
   184	
   185	## 6. Nutrient dictionary
   186	
   187	Map each source's nutrients onto a canonical set, and keep both sides.
   188	
   189	- Canonical: `nutrient_id`, name, unit, and a stable code.
   190	- Mapping: `(source, source_nutrient_id) → nutrient_id`, held as data, not code.
   191	- Never discard `source_nutrient_id`, `source_unit`, or the source's own name.
   192	
   193	USDA alone defines 477 nutrients; CoFID splits across seven sheets by family;
   194	CIQUAL uses `const_code`. The mapping table will be wrong in places on the first
   195	pass. Keeping it as data means fixing it is an update, not a re-extraction.
   196	
   197	**Do not deduplicate foods across sources in v1.** Four tables describing "raw
   198	carrot" is not a defect — the values differ legitimately by country, cultivar and
   199	method. Cross-source matching is a search and ranking problem, not a merge
   200	problem, and merging is irreversible.
   201	
   202	---
   203	
   204	## 7. Branded foods — one decision, deferred deliberately
   205	
   206	Branded Foods is **1,999,950 of USDA's 2,101,280 rows — 95%** — and is
   207	manufacturer-declared label data, not laboratory analysis. It is CC0, so there
   208	is no rights question. There is a product question:
   209	
   210	| | Ship Branded Foods in v1 | Hold to v2 |
   211	|---|---|---|
   212	| Barcode scanning | works out of the box | needs another source |
   213	| Bundle size | large; 27.2 M nutrient rows total | ~100 k foods, small |
   214	| Data quality | label-declared, ~15 panel nutrients | analytical, full profiles |
   215	| Search quality | 2 M near-duplicate brand strings to rank against | clean |
   216	
   217	Not a decision for this document. It is flagged because bundle size and search
   218	ranking are both downstream of it, and both are expensive to redo.
   219	
   220	---
   221	
   222	## 8. Build order
   223	
   224	Aligned to Technical Spec v1.0 Slice 1, which already calls for provenance enums:
   225	
   226	1. **Nutrient dictionary + qualifier enum.** Data, not code. Nothing else is
   227	   designable until the value model is fixed.
   228	2. **Extract USDA.** Already relational and CC0 — the lowest-risk first target,
   229	   and it exercises portions, derivations and the qualifier path in one go.
   230	3. **Canonicalise USDA.** Proves the schema against 27.2 M values.
   231	4. **Bundle step with the failing licence assertion**, before a second source
   232	   exists. Build the guard while the thing it guards is still trivial.
   233	5. **Extract + canonicalise CIQUAL, CoFID, AFCD.** Three sources, three
   234	   qualifier vocabularies — this is where the value model earns its keep.
   235	6. **Attribution manifest**, generated from `DATASETS.csv`, shipped in-app.
   236	   CC BY and OGL both require it; generating it means it cannot drift.
   237	
   238	---
   239	
   240	## 9. Open questions
   241	
   242	1. Branded Foods in v1 — §7.
   243	2. Canonical nutrient set: adopt USDA's 477 as the spine, or define a smaller
   244	   Almanac set and map everything into it?
   245	3. Does Almanac need CoFID's `Tr` shown to users as "trace", or is
   246	   `qualifier != measured` enough for the UI to grey a value out?
   247	4. Arabic/Gulf coverage stays a build problem — Almanac-native records under the
   248	   `almanac:` namespace. Unblocked by none of the pending emails.
   249	
   250	---
   251	
   252	*Nothing in this document has been executed. `processed/` is empty, `raw/` is
   253	verified intact, and no dataset has been merged, renamed, translated,
   254	unit-converted, deduplicated or transformed.*
